name: Chapter 4: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
description: Lewis structures, formal charge, ionic bonds, bond parameters, resonance, dipole moment, VSEPR, hybridisation, MO theory, hydrogen bonds

cards.term: What is a chemical bond?
cards.definition: The attractive force that holds the constituents (atoms, ions, etc.) together in a chemical species

cards.term: Why do atoms form bonds at all?
cards.definition: Bonding is nature’s way of lowering the energy of the system to attain stability

cards.term: Name the four theories of bonding in this unit.
cards.definition: Kössel–Lewis approach, VSEPR theory, valence bond (VB) theory and molecular orbital (MO) theory

cards.term: Who first explained valence in terms of electrons, and when?
cards.definition: Kössel and Lewis independently, in 1916, based on the inertness of noble gases

cards.term: What was the Lewis "kernel"?
cards.definition: The nucleus + inner electrons of an atom (positively charged)

cards.term: How did Lewis picture the octet?
cards.definition:
Eight outer electrons at the corners of a cube around the kernel.
Na: one corner filled; a noble gas: all eight

cards.term: What do the dots in a Lewis symbol stand for?
cards.definition: The valence electrons (inner electrons are well protected and do not take part)

cards.term: How do you get the group valence from a Lewis symbol?
cards.definition: Number of dots, or 8 − number of dots

cards.term: Kössel’s postulates on ionic bonding
cards.definition: Periodic table: halogens and alkali metals are separated by the noble gases; Ion formation: halogen gains an e⁻ (anion); alkali metal loses one (cation); Ions formed: attain the stable noble-gas configuration ns²np⁶ (He: duplet); Stability: the ions are held by electrostatic attraction

cards.term: Kössel: how does NaCl form?
cards.definition: Na [Ne]3s¹ → Na⁺ [Ne] + e⁻ Cl [Ne]3s²3p⁵ + e⁻ → Cl⁻ [Ar] Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → Na⁺Cl⁻

cards.term: What is electrovalence?
cards.definition: The number of unit charges on the ion (Ca²⁺: +2, Cl⁻: −1)

cards.text: Octet rule (Kössel and Lewis, 1916): atoms combine by {{c1::transfer}} or {{c2::sharing}} of valence electrons so as to have an {{c3::octet}} in their valence shells.

cards.term: Who introduced the term "covalent bond", and what did he drop from Lewis’s model?
cards.definition: Langmuir (1919); he abandoned the idea of a stationary cubical octet

cards.term: Conditions for a covalent bond (Lewis–Langmuir)
cards.definition: 1: each bond = sharing of an electron pair; 2: each atom contributes at least one electron to the pair; 3: atoms attain noble-gas configurations by sharing

cards.term: Name molecules with a double bond and with a triple bond.
cards.definition: Double: CO₂ (two C=O), C₂H₄. Triple: N₂, C₂H₂

cards.term: Steps for writing a Lewis structure
cards.definition: 1: add the valence electrons of all atoms; 2: add 1 e⁻ per negative charge; subtract 1 per positive charge; 3: put the least electronegative atom in the centre; 4: single bonds first, then complete octets on terminal atoms; 5: leftover pairs → multiple bonds or lone pairs

cards.term: Which atom usually goes in the centre of a Lewis structure? Give examples.
cards.definition: The least electronegative: N in NF₃, C in CO₃²⁻

cards.term: How many valence electrons for CO₃²⁻, and for NH₄⁺?
cards.definition: CO₃²⁻: 4 + 18 + 2 = 24. NH₄⁺: 5 + 4 − 1 = 8

cards.term: Problem 4.1: Lewis structure of CO?
cards.definition: 10 valence e⁻; a single bond leaves C short of an octet, so C≡O with one lone pair on each atom

cards.term: Problem 4.2: Lewis structure of NO₂⁻?
cards.definition: 18 e⁻ one N=O, one N–O⁻, one lone pair on N the double bond can be on either O (two structures)

cards.term: Lewis structure of O₃?
cards.definition: Central O: one O=O and one O–O; formal charges +1 (centre), 0, −1

cards.term: Lewis structure of NF₃?
cards.definition: N with three N–F single bonds and one lone pair

cards.term: Lewis structure of CO₃²⁻?
cards.definition: C with one C=O and two C–O⁻; overall charge 2−

cards.term: Lewis structure of HNO₃?
cards.definition: N⁺ bonded to one =O, one –O⁻ and one –OH

cards.term: Exercise 4.20: correct Lewis structure of acetic acid, CH₃COOH?
cards.definition: H₃C–C(=O)–O–H: the carboxyl C has one C=O and one C–OH; each O keeps two lone pairs

cards.term: Formula for formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure?
cards.definition:
\[FC = V - L - \tfrac12 S\]
V = valence e⁻ of the free atom, L = lone-pair e⁻, S = shared e⁻

cards.term: What assumption lies behind counting formal charge?
cards.definition: The atom owns one electron of each shared pair and both electrons of its lone pairs

cards.term: Formal charges on the three O atoms of O₃?
cards.definition: Central O: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1 double-bonded end O: 0 single-bonded end O: 6 − 6 − 1 = −1

cards.term: Which Lewis structure is usually the lowest-energy one?
cards.definition: The one with the smallest formal charges on the atoms

cards.term: Do formal charges show real charge separation?
cards.definition: No. They only keep track of valence electrons, on a purely covalent (equal-sharing) view

cards.term: Three types of exceptions to the octet rule?
cards.definition: Incomplete octet of the central atom, odd-electron molecules, expanded octet

cards.term: Incomplete octet: examples and reason?
cards.definition: LiCl, BeH₂, BCl₃ (also AlCl₃, BF₃): Li, Be and B have fewer than four valence electrons (1, 2, 3)

cards.term: Give two odd-electron molecules.
cards.definition: NO and NO₂

cards.term: Why can elements of the third period and beyond have an expanded octet?
cards.definition: They have d orbitals available for bonding besides s and p

cards.term: Give three examples of an expanded octet.
cards.definition: PF₅ (10 e⁻), SF₆ (12 e⁻), H₂SO₄ (12 e⁻ around S), plus many coordination compounds

cards.term: Name a sulphur compound in which S obeys the octet rule.
cards.definition: SCl₂ (sulphur dichloride)

cards.term: Which compounds challenge the octet rule’s basis (noble-gas inertness)?
cards.definition: XeF₂, KrF₂, XeOF₂: xenon and krypton do combine with O and F

cards.term: Two more drawbacks of the octet theory?
cards.definition: It does not explain shapes of molecules, and says nothing about their energy (relative stability)

cards.term: Formation of an ionic compound depends mainly on which two things?
cards.definition: The ease of forming the ions from neutral atoms, and the arrangement of ions in the crystal lattice

cards.term: Exercise 4.6: favourable factors for an ionic bond?
cards.definition:
Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
Highly negative electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal
High lattice enthalpy

cards.term: Is ionisation always endothermic? Electron gain?
cards.definition: Ionisation: always endothermic. Electron gain: can be exothermic or endothermic

cards.term: Electron affinity vs electron gain enthalpy?
cards.definition: Electron affinity is the negative of the energy change on electron gain

cards.term: Which common cation contains only non-metals?
cards.definition: NH₄⁺ (ammonium)

cards.term: Name the crystal structure of NaCl.
cards.definition: Rock salt structure: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ alternate in three dimensions

cards.term: Na → Na⁺ costs 495.8 kJ/mol and Cl → Cl⁻ releases only 348.7 kJ/mol. Why does NaCl still form?
cards.definition: The lattice enthalpy (788 kJ mol⁻¹) more than makes up the net 147.1 kJ mol⁻¹ absorbed

cards.term: What truly measures the stability of an ionic compound?
cards.definition: Its enthalpy of lattice formation, not simply reaching an octet in the gaseous ions

cards.term: Define lattice enthalpy.
cards.definition: Energy needed to completely separate 1 mol of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions (to infinite distance)

cards.term: Why can lattice enthalpy not be found just from attractions and repulsions between ion pairs?
cards.definition: The crystal is three-dimensional; factors of the crystal geometry must be included

cards.term:
Exercise 4.14: show electron transfer to form ions for (a) K and S
(b) Ca and O
(c) Al and N.
cards.definition: (a) 2K → 2K⁺ + 2e⁻; S + 2e⁻ → S²⁻ → K₂S. (b) Ca²⁺ + O²⁻ → CaO. (c) Al³⁺ + N³⁻ → AlN

cards.term: Exercise 4.3: Lewis symbols for S and S²⁻, Al and Al³⁺, H and H⁻?
cards.definition: S: 6 dots S²⁻: 8 dots. Al: 3 dots Al³⁺: no dots. H: 1 dot H⁻: 2 dots

cards.term: Define bond length.
cards.definition:
The equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms in a molecule.
Measured by spectroscopy, X-ray and electron diffraction

cards.term: Bond length R of AB in terms of covalent radii?

cards.text: Covalent radius is half the distance between two similar atoms joined by a covalent bond {{c1::in the same molecule}}; van der Waals radius is half the distance between two similar atoms {{c2::in separate molecules}} in a solid.

cards.term: What does the van der Waals radius represent?
cards.definition: The overall size of the atom, including its valence shell, in a non-bonded situation

cards.term: Fig. 4.2 · Covalent and van der Waals radii of chlorine
Which is larger for chlorine: covalent or van der Waals radius?
cards.definition: van der Waals (180 pm vs 99 pm)

cards.term: Trend: why does the H–X bond length rise from HF to HI?
cards.definition: The halogen atom gets bigger down the group (larger covalent radius)

cards.term: Define bond angle.
cards.definition: The angle between the orbitals containing bonding electron pairs around the central atom; found by spectroscopy

cards.term: H–O–H bond angle in water?
cards.definition: 104.5°

cards.term: Define bond enthalpy.
cards.definition: Energy needed to break 1 mol of bonds of a particular type between two atoms in the gaseous state (kJ mol⁻¹)

cards.term: Bond enthalpies: H2, O2, N2, HCl

cards.term: Larger bond dissociation enthalpy means…?
cards.definition: A stronger bond

cards.term: Why is the second O–H bond of water broken with a different energy from the first (502 vs 427 kJ/mol)?
cards.definition: After the first break, the chemical environment of the remaining O–H has changed

cards.term: Average O–H bond enthalpy in water?
cards.definition: \[\dfrac{502 + 427}{2} =\]464.5 kJ mol⁻¹: total dissociation enthalpy ÷ number of bonds broken

cards.term: Bond order in the Lewis picture?
cards.definition: The number of bonds (shared pairs) between the two atoms: H₂ 1, O₂ 2, N₂ 3, CO 3

cards.term: Which species share bond order 3 by being isoelectronic?
cards.definition: N₂, CO, NO⁺

cards.term: Which species share bond order 1 by being isoelectronic?
cards.definition: F₂ and O₂²⁻

cards.term: What is special about N₂’s bond enthalpy?
cards.definition: 946 kJ mol⁻¹: one of the highest for a diatomic molecule (triple bond)

cards.text: As bond order increases, bond enthalpy {{c1::increases}} and bond length {{c2::decreases}}.

cards.term: Exercise 4.9: express bond strength in terms of bond order.
cards.definition: Higher bond order → stronger bond (higher bond enthalpy) and shorter bond

cards.term: Both O–O bonds in O₃ are 128 pm. How does this compare with single and double bonds?
cards.definition: Between O–O (148 pm) and O=O (121 pm): neither Lewis structure fits alone

cards.term: State the concept of resonance.
cards.definition:
When one Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, several canonical structures are written.
They have similar energy, the same positions of nuclei and the same bonding/non-bonding pairs.
Their hybrid is the real molecule

cards.term: How is resonance shown?
cards.definition: With a double-headed arrow (↔)

cards.term: Resonance energy?
cards.definition: Energy of the most stable canonical structure − energy of the resonance hybrid: resonance stabilises the molecule

cards.term: Do canonical forms really exist?
cards.definition:
No.
The molecule does not flip between them.
They have no real existence, and there is no equilibrium between them

cards.term: Problem 4.3: why is CO₃²⁻ a resonance hybrid?
cards.definition: One Lewis structure shows unequal bonds, but all C–O bonds are found equivalent: three canonical forms

cards.term: Problem 4.4: C–O length in CO₂ (115 pm) lies between which values?
cards.definition: C=O 121 pm and C≡O 110 pm: CO₂ is a hybrid of three forms

cards.term: Exercise 4.12: two structures of H₃PO₃ differ in where an H sits (on P or on O). Are they canonical forms?
cards.definition: No: canonical forms must have the same positions of nuclei and differ only in electrons

cards.term: Exercise 4.13: how many resonance structures for SO₃, NO₂ and NO₃⁻?
cards.definition: SO₃: 3 (one S=O moving); NO₂: 2; NO₃⁻: 3 (one N=O moving)

cards.term: Which is a non-polar covalent bond: H–H or H–F?
cards.definition: H–H (identical atoms share equally); H–F is polar (Exercise 4.18)

cards.term: Formula and unit of dipole moment?
cards.definition:
\[\mu = Q \times r\]
Unit: debye (D), 1 D = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m

cards.term: Is dipole moment a scalar or a vector?
cards.definition: Vector: for a polyatomic molecule it is the vector sum of bond dipoles

cards.term: The chemist’s crossed arrow for a dipole: where are the cross and the head?
cards.definition: Cross on the positive end, head on the negative end

cards.term: Dipole moment of H₂O?
cards.definition: 1.85 D (bent, H–O–H 104.5°)

cards.term: Exercise 4.22: why is μ of BeH₂ (or BeF₂) zero though the bonds are polar?
cards.definition: The molecule is linear: two equal bond dipoles point opposite and cancel

cards.term: Exercise 4.15: CO₂ and H₂O are both triatomic. Why is μ(CO₂) = 0 but μ(H₂O) = 1.85 D?
cards.definition: CO₂ is linear (bond dipoles cancel); H₂O is bent (they add)

cards.term: Why is μ of BF₃ zero though B–F bonds are polar?
cards.definition: Trigonal planar at 120°: the three bond moments sum to zero

cards.term: Exercise 4.23: why is μ(NH₃) greater than μ(NF₃)?
cards.definition:
In NH₃ the lone-pair dipole points the same way as the N–H bond moments.
In NF₃ it points opposite to the N–F moments

cards.term: Exercise 4.16: uses of dipole moment?
cards.definition:
To tell polar from non-polar molecules
To predict shape (e.g. linear CO₂ vs bent H₂O)
To estimate the % ionic character of a bond

cards.term: Exercise 4.17: electronegativity vs electron gain enthalpy?
cards.definition: Electronegativity: tendency of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair; relative, no unit. Electron gain enthalpy: energy change when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron; measurable, kJ mol⁻¹

cards.term: Exercise 4.19: arrange in increasing ionic character: LiF, K₂O, N₂, SO₂, ClF.
cards.definition: N₂ < SO₂ < ClF < K₂O < LiF (by electronegativity difference: 0, 1.0, 1.0, 2.7, 3.0)

cards.term: Do ionic bonds have covalent character?
cards.definition:
Yes: just as covalent bonds have partial ionic character, ionic bonds have partial covalent character.
The cation polarises the anion

cards.text: Fajans’ rules: covalent character of an ionic bond increases with a {{c1::smaller}} cation, a {{c2::larger}} anion, and a {{c3::greater charge}} on the cation.

cards.term: For the same size and charge, which cation polarises more: (n−1)dⁿns⁰ (transition metal) or ns²np⁶ (noble-gas core)?
cards.definition: (n−1)dⁿns⁰: d electrons shield the nucleus poorly

cards.term: Intuition: why does a small, highly charged cation make a bond covalent?
cards.definition:
Its concentrated positive charge pulls the anion’s electron cloud towards itself.
Electron density builds up between the nuclei, like a shared pair

cards.term: Who proposed VSEPR theory, and who refined it?
cards.definition: Sidgwick and Powell (1940); refined by Nyholm and Gillespie (1957)

cards.term: Postulates of VSEPR theory
cards.definition: Shape depends on: the number of valence-shell electron pairs (bonded or not) around the central atom; Electron pairs: repel one another (their clouds are negative); They take positions that: minimise repulsion (maximise distance); Valence shell is taken as: a sphere, pairs on its surface far apart; A multiple bond counts as: one "super pair"; With resonance: VSEPR applies to any canonical structure

cards.term: Order of electron-pair repulsions?
cards.definition: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp

cards.term: Why do lone pairs repel more than bond pairs (Nyholm and Gillespie)?
cards.definition:
A lone pair is localised on one atom only; a bond pair is shared between two.
So the lone pair occupies more space

cards.term: What do extra lone-pair repulsions do to shapes?
cards.definition: They cause deviations from idealised shapes and alter bond angles

cards.term: Exercise 4.7: shapes by VSEPR of BeCl₂, BCl₃, SiCl₄, AsF₅, H₂S, PH₃?
cards.definition: Linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, bent, trigonal pyramidal

cards.term: H–N–H angle in NH₃, and why not 109.5°?
cards.definition: 107°: lp–bp repulsion > bp–bp squeezes the bond pairs

cards.term: Exercise 4.8: both NH₃ and H₂O are distorted tetrahedral. Why is the angle smaller in water (104.5° vs 107°)?
cards.definition: H₂O has two lone pairs; the extra lp–lp repulsion (strongest) squeezes the O–H bonds more

cards.term: In SF₄, is the lone pair axial or equatorial, and why?
cards.definition: Equatorial: only two lp–bp repulsions at 90° (vs three if axial) → see-saw

cards.term: In ClF₃, where do the two lone pairs sit?
cards.definition: Equatorial positions, giving a T-shape

cards.term: In XeF₄, where are the two lone pairs?
cards.definition: Opposite each other (180°) → square planar

cards.term: For which compounds does VSEPR predict shapes especially well?
cards.definition: p-block compounds; its theoretical basis is still debated

cards.term: Trap: shape vs electron geometry of NH₃?
cards.definition:
Electron-pair geometry: tetrahedral
Shape (atoms only): trigonal pyramidal
Lone pairs are invisible in the shape

cards.term: Who introduced valence bond theory?
cards.definition: Heitler and London (1927), developed by Pauling

cards.term: Exercise 4.33: why does H₂ form as two H atoms approach (VB theory)?
cards.definition:
New attractions (nucleus–other electron) and repulsions arise.
Attraction wins, and the energy falls to a minimum at the bond length

cards.term: Bond length and bond enthalpy of H₂ (VB section)?
cards.definition: 74 pm; 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ released on forming 1 mol

cards.term: Intuition: why does the energy curve for H₂ rise again at very short distance?
cards.definition: Nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions grow faster than attraction; the minimum is the bond length

cards.term: Orbital overlap concept?
cards.definition:
A covalent bond forms by partial merging (overlap) of half-filled valence orbitals with opposite spins.
The greater the overlap, the stronger the bond

cards.term: Exercise 4.37: significance of the + and − signs on orbital lobes?
cards.definition: They are the phase (sign) of the wave function, not charge. Same-sign overlap → bond; opposite sign → no bond

cards.term: What H–C–H angle would simple (unhybridised) overlap predict for CH₄?
cards.definition: 90° (real: 109.5°); simple overlap cannot explain directional shapes, so hybridisation is needed

cards.term: How is a σ bond formed?
cards.definition: Head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis

cards.term: Which overlaps can give a σ bond?
cards.definition: s–s, s–p, p–p (head-on)

cards.term: How is a π bond formed?
cards.definition: Sidewise overlap: orbital axes parallel, perpendicular to the internuclear axis; two lobes, above and below

cards.term: Which is stronger, σ or π, and why?
cards.definition: σ: larger extent of overlap

cards.term: Can a π bond exist without a σ bond between two atoms?
cards.definition: No. π bonds form in addition to a σ bond (NCERT’s rule; C₂ in MO theory is the exception)

cards.term: Exercise 4.29: with x as the internuclear axis, which will not form a σ bond: 1s+1s, 1s+2pₓ, 2p<sub>y</sub>+2p<sub>y</sub>, 1s+2s?
cards.definition: 2py + 2py (sidewise → π)

cards.term: Exercise 4.28: σ and π bonds in C₂H₂ and C₂H₄?
cards.definition: C₂H₂: 3σ, 2π; C₂H₄: 5σ, 1π

cards.term: Exercise 4.31: bond pairs and lone pairs in H₂O?
cards.definition: 2 bond pairs (O–H) and 2 lone pairs on O

cards.term: Who introduced hybridisation, and why?
cards.definition: Pauling, to explain the characteristic shapes of polyatomic molecules (e.g. CH₄, NH₃, H₂O)

cards.term: Define hybridisation.
cards.definition: Intermixing of orbitals of slightly different energies to form a new set of orbitals of equivalent energy and shape

cards.term: How many hybrid orbitals form from n atomic orbitals?
cards.definition: n (always equal)

cards.term: Can filled orbitals take part in hybridisation?
cards.definition: Yes; not only half-filled ones

cards.term: sp, sp2, sp3: s-character and angle
cards.definition: sp: 50% s · 180° · linear; sp²: 33% s · 120° · trigonal planar; sp³: 25% s · 109.5° · tetrahedral

cards.definition: sp², trigonal planar (120°)

cards.term: Hybridisation and shape of CH₄?
cards.definition: sp³, tetrahedral (109.5°)

cards.term: Exercise 4.21: why is CH₄ tetrahedral and not square planar?
cards.definition: sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5°, least repulsion). Square planar needs 90° angles (more repulsion) and dsp² orbitals, which C (no d orbitals) cannot form

cards.term: Hybridisation and shape of NH₃?
cards.definition: sp³ N with one lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, 107°

cards.term: Hybridisation and shape of H₂O?
cards.definition: sp³ O with two lone pairs: bent (V-shape), 104.5°

cards.term: Intuition: more s-character in a hybrid means…?
cards.definition:
A shorter, stronger bond
A wider angle (sp 180° > sp² 120° > sp³ 109.5°)
A more electronegative carbon

cards.term: Ethane: C–C and C–H bond lengths?
cards.definition: C–C 154 pm (sp³–sp³ σ); C–H 109 pm

cards.term: Ethene: what makes up the C=C bond?
cards.definition: One sp²–sp² σ + one π (from the unhybridised 2p orbitals); C=C 134 pm

cards.term: Bond angles in ethene?
cards.definition: H–C–H 117.6°; H–C–C 121°

cards.term: What makes up the C≡C bond in ethyne?
cards.definition: 1 σ (sp–sp) + 2 π; molecule linear

cards.term: Exercise 4.30: hybrid orbitals used by carbon in CH₃–CH=CH₂, CH₃–CH₂–OH, CH₃CHO, CH₃COOH?
cards.definition: CH₃–CH=CH₂: sp³, sp², sp². Ethanol: sp³, sp³. CH₃CHO: sp³, sp². CH₃COOH: sp³, sp²

cards.term: Shortcut: hybridisation of carbon from its bonds?
cards.definition: Four single bonds → sp³ one double bond → sp² a triple bond or two double bonds → sp

cards.term: Why can third-period atoms use d orbitals but 3p–3d–4s hybridisation of nitrogen is impossible?
cards.definition:
Second-period atoms have no d orbitals.
In the third period, 3s, 3p and 3d are close in energy (while 3p and 4s differ a lot)

cards.term: d-orbital hybridisation: shapes and examples
cards.definition: sp³d: trigonal bipyramidal · PCl₅; sp³d²: octahedral · SF₆ (square pyramidal BrF₅); dsp²: square planar · [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻; d²sp³: octahedral · [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺

cards.term: Exercise 4.38: hybridisation of PCl₅, and why are the axial bonds longer?
cards.definition:
sp³d
The two axial bond pairs suffer more repulsion (three equatorial pairs at 90°), so they are longer and weaker

cards.term: Why is PCl₅ reactive?
cards.definition: Its axial bonds are longer and weaker; a Cl is easily lost (PCl₅ → PCl₃ + Cl₂)

cards.term: Hybridisation and geometry of SF₆?
cards.definition: sp³d², regular octahedral; six S–F bonds at 90°

cards.term: Exercise 4.25: AlCl₃ + Cl⁻ → AlCl₄⁻. Change in the hybridisation of Al?
cards.definition: sp² (trigonal planar) → sp³ (tetrahedral)

cards.term: Exercise 4.26: BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃. Change in hybridisation of B and N?
cards.definition: B: sp² → sp³; N: stays sp³ (its lone pair becomes a bond pair)

cards.term: Who developed molecular orbital theory?
cards.definition: F. Hund and R.S. Mulliken (1932)

cards.term: Salient features of MO theory
cards.definition: Electrons in a molecule are in: molecular orbitals; AOs combined must have: comparable energy and proper symmetry; An AO is influenced by: one nucleus (monocentric); An MO is influenced by: two or more nuclei (polycentric); Number of MOs formed: equals number of AOs combined; Bonding MO vs antibonding: lower energy, more stable; Filling order: aufbau, Pauli, Hund

cards.term: LCAO expressions for σ and σ*?
cards.definition: \[\sigma = \psi_A + \psi_B,\quad \sigma^* = \psi_A - \psi_B\]

cards.text: A bonding MO forms by {{c1::constructive}} interference (addition) of electron waves; an antibonding MO by {{c2::destructive}} interference (subtraction).

cards.term: Why is a bonding MO lower in energy than the AOs, and antibonding higher?
cards.definition: Bonding: electron density builds between the nuclei and holds them. Antibonding: density is pushed away, leaving a nodal plane; the nuclei repel

cards.text: Exercise 4.34: conditions for LCAO: combining AOs must have {{c1::the same or nearly the same energy}}, {{c2::the same symmetry about the molecular axis}}, and {{c3::maximum overlap}}.

cards.term: Can 1s combine with 2s? Can 2p<sub>z</sub> of one atom combine with 2pₓ of the other (z = molecular axis)?
cards.definition: No to both: 1s and 2s differ in energy; 2pz and 2pₓ differ in symmetry

cards.term: Which MOs are symmetrical about the bond axis: σ or π?
cards.definition: σ (π are not)

cards.term: Fig. 4.20 · Name each molecular orbital

cards.text: For {{c1::B₂, C₂ and N₂}}, the π2pₓ and π2p<sub>y</sub> MOs lie {{c2::below}} σ2p<sub>z</sub>; for O₂ and F₂, σ2p<sub>z</sub> lies below π2p.

cards.term: Mnemonic: when does σ2pz drop below π2p?
cards.definition: From O₂ onwards (O₂, F₂, Ne₂). Up to N₂, s–p mixing pushes σ2pz above π2p

cards.term: Bond order formula in MO theory?
cards.definition: B.O. = \( \tfrac12 (N_b - N_a) \) (N<sub>b</sub>, N<sub>a</sub> = electrons in bonding and antibonding MOs)

cards.term: Interpreting MO electronic configurations
cards.definition: N_b > N_a (positive B.O.): stable molecule; N_b ≤ N_a (zero or negative): unstable, does not exist; B.O. 1, 2, 3: single, double, triple bond; Higher B.O.: shorter bond; All MOs doubly filled: diamagnetic; Any MO singly filled: paramagnetic

cards.definition: \( (\sigma 1s)^2 \); B.O. = (2 − 0)/2 = 1; diamagnetic

cards.term: Correction: NCERT gives H₂’s bond energy as 435.8 kJ/mol in 4.3.3 but 438 kJ/mol in 4.8. Which to use?
cards.definition: Two slightly different quoted values for the same quantity. For bond-enthalpy questions use 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ (4.3.3); the bond length 74 pm is the same in both

cards.term: Bond order of He₂, and does it exist?
cards.definition: σ1s² σ*1s² → ½(2 − 2) = 0, so it does not exist

cards.term: Exercise 4.35: use MO theory to show why Be₂ does not exist.
cards.definition: Be₂: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² → Nb = Na = 4, B.O. = 0

cards.term: Li₂: configuration, bond order, magnetism?
cards.definition: KK(σ2s)² → B.O. 1; diamagnetic (known in the vapour phase)

cards.term: What does "KK" mean in KK(σ2s)²?
cards.definition: The closed K-shell part (σ1s)² (σ*1s)²

cards.term: What is unusual about the double bond in C₂?
cards.definition: Both bonds are π bonds (four electrons in π2pₓ and π2py), not σ + π; C₂ is diamagnetic

cards.term: Correction: NCERT writes C₂ as (σ1s)²(σ*1s)²(σ*2s)²(π2pₓ² = π2py²). What is missing?
cards.definition: The (σ2s)² term: only 10 of the 12 electrons are shown. Correct: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2pₓ² π2py² (as in the KK form on the next line)

cards.definition: 3, 2, 2.5, 1.5

cards.term: Shortcut: bond order of 2nd-period diatomic species from the electron count?
cards.definition:
It peaks at 3 for 10 electrons (N₂, CO, NO⁺) and falls by 0.5 per electron either side.
8 → 2 (C₂), 12 → 2 (O₂), 14 → 1 (F₂), 6 → 1 (B₂)

cards.term: Removing an electron from O₂ raises the bond order but from N₂ lowers it. Why?
cards.definition: O₂ loses an antibonding (π*) electron → B.O. 2.5. N₂ loses a bonding electron → B.O. 2.5 from 3

cards.term: To which atoms must H be bonded to form hydrogen bonds?
cards.definition: Highly electronegative F, O or N

cards.term: Exercise 4.39: define hydrogen bond. Weaker or stronger than van der Waals forces?
cards.definition:
The attractive force binding the H atom of one molecule to an electronegative atom (F, O, N) of another.
Stronger than van der Waals forces, weaker than covalent bonds

cards.term: Cause of hydrogen bonding?
cards.definition:
The shared pair shifts towards the electronegative X, leaving H with δ+.
This H is attracted by the δ− X of a neighbour:
Hδ+–Xδ− ··· Hδ+–Xδ−

cards.term: How is a hydrogen bond drawn?
cards.definition: With a dotted line (···); the covalent bond is a solid line. H acts as a bridge between two atoms

cards.term: In which physical state is hydrogen bonding strongest?
cards.definition: Solid (maximum); weakest in the gas

cards.term: Types of hydrogen bond?
cards.definition: Intermolecular (between molecules) and intramolecular (within one molecule)

cards.term: Give examples of intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
cards.definition: HF (zig-zag chains), water, alcohols

cards.term: Give an example of intramolecular hydrogen bonding.
cards.definition: o-Nitrophenol (H between the two O atoms)

cards.term: Intuition: why does o-nitrophenol boil lower than p-nitrophenol?
cards.definition:
Its H-bond is intramolecular (inside one molecule), so molecules do not stick together.
p-Nitrophenol forms intermolecular H-bonds

cards.term: Why is water a liquid while H₂S is a gas at room temperature?
cards.definition: Water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds; S is not electronegative enough for strong H-bonding

cards.term: Bonding theories and what they explain
cards.definition: Kössel: ionic bonds via noble-gas ions; Lewis–Langmuir: covalent bonds by electron sharing; VSEPR: shapes from electron-pair repulsion; VB + hybridisation: directional bonds, σ and π; MO theory: bond order, magnetism (O₂ paramagnetic)
